title: Podman Desktop consumes increasing CPU and memory while idle on Windows
body: I updated Podman and Podman Desktop on my Windows 11 machine, and Podman Desktop 1.14.2 now consistently uses 20–30% CPU and up to 4 GB of memory while doing nothing. I have no images or containers in use. After it runs for a while, the UI becomes very sluggish and nearly unresponsive, and my PC's fans run at full speed. I installed it using Scoop. Is this expected?

symptoms_visible: While idle, Podman Desktop uses 20–30% CPU and its memory grows as high as 4 GB.
After running for a while, the UI becomes very sluggish and nearly unresponsive, and my PC's fans run at full speed.
N0.label: N0 idle resource growth reported

symptoms_visible: Podman Desktop's CPU and memory continue increasing even though the WSL Podman machine shows very low CPU usage and I have no other container or Kubernetes environment running.
N1.label: N1 environment and VM state established

symptoms_visible: Starting near 300 MB, Podman Desktop keeps growing toward 1 GB and beyond while its CPU usage rises.
The logs repeatedly print connection errors for the podman-machine-default pipe followed by 'Will reconnect in 5s'.
Restarting Podman Desktop, WSL2, or the whole machine does not prevent the same CPU and memory growth from returning after 30–60 minutes.
N2.label: N2 recurring connection errors captured

symptoms_visible: With every extension disabled, Podman Desktop remains normal; enabling only the Podman extension and starting the machine brings back the repeated errors and increasing CPU and memory use.
The Podman machine reports 100% idle CPU and about 554 MiB used memory while the Windows Podman Desktop process is consuming resources.
A second Windows laptop develops the same repeated pipe errors and reaches almost 4 GB of memory and about 40% CPU.
N3.label: N3 Podman integration isolated

symptoms_visible: With the Windows firewall disabled, the repeated pipe errors and increasing Podman Desktop CPU and memory use are unchanged.
N3_x.label: N3_x firewall-disable aftermath

symptoms_visible: After reverting Podman Desktop to 1.13.3, the repeated errors and high CPU and memory consumption still occur.
N4_x.label: N4_x Podman Desktop downgrade aftermath

symptoms_visible: After reverting Podman from 5.3.1 to 5.2.5, the pipe errors no longer appear and Podman Desktop no longer consumes increasing CPU or memory while idle.
N5.label: N5 Podman engine downgrade verified

symptoms_visible: Podman Desktop remains responsive without repeated pipe errors or increasing idle CPU and memory use after the Podman engine downgrade.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved by Podman engine downgrade

question_patterns: Is the Podman machine running, and is it using WSL or Hyper-V?
How is your Podman machine configured?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, the Podman machine is running. It is on WSL, and I configured it in rootless mode.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I do not have a Podman machine running; the resource use starts with Podman Desktop alone.
The machine is running under Hyper-V rather than WSL, but otherwise the behavior is identical.

question_patterns: Do you have kind, Docker, OpenShift Local, or an active Kubernetes context running?
What other container or Kubernetes environments are active?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have nothing else running: no kind, Docker, OpenShift Local, or Kubernetes cluster.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I have several active Kubernetes clusters and the load stops when I remove their contexts.

question_patterns: Does top inside the Podman machine show any busy process?
Is the resource use also visible inside the VM?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: A top inside podman-machine-default shows almost nothing happening and very low CPU usage.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's system only, from c0-c4: the reporter confirms a rootless WSL Podman machine, no other listed environments, and low activity inside the VM. The seven c3 images are attached to the setup facts they support.

question_patterns: Can you monitor the Podman Desktop process while its memory grows and share what it is doing?
Could you capture a Process Monitor trace during the resource increase?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tracked it with Process Monitor. It grew from about 300 MB toward 1 GB before I stopped tracking, and it seemed to spend most of its time reading app.asar. I uploaded the PML trace.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The memory stays around 300 MB for several hours and the trace shows no repeated activity.

question_patterns: Can you check the Podman Desktop logs for recurring errors?
What appears repeatedly in the logs while CPU and memory are increasing?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The logs repeatedly say `connect ENOENT \\.\pipe\podman-machine-default`, `Error when handling events`, and `Will reconnect in 5s`. They also sometimes say there is no running provider for the matching container or that the engine has no API.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The logs remain quiet while memory grows; there are no connection or retry errors.
The same pipe error repeats, but the retry message says ten seconds rather than five.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's system, c6-c15: after being asked for logs, the reporter supplies a Process Monitor trace, raw error lines, and later volunteers that restarts only delay the same growth. The reporter's speculation that logs may be accumulating is not encoded as a conclusion.

question_patterns: Can you disable all extensions and then enable them one at a time to see which state triggers the resource use?
Does the behavior change when the Podman extension is disabled?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With everything disabled, I have no problem. When I enable only the Podman extension and start the Podman machine, the errors begin and CPU and memory pressure increase until it becomes unbearable.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The resource growth continues with every extension disabled and before the Podman machine starts.

question_patterns: What happens if every extension is disabled?
Does Podman Desktop remain stable with extensions turned off?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: When all extensions are disabled, the problem does not occur.

question_patterns: Please run `podman machine ssh top -b -n 1` and `podman machine ssh free -h`; what is the raw output?
How much CPU and memory is the Podman machine itself using?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The machine reports 100.0% idle CPU. It has about 7.7 GiB total memory, about 554 MiB used, 7.2 GiB available, and no swap in use.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The machine itself is at 100% CPU with nearly all 7.7 GiB of memory in use.
The machine is still idle, but it reports about 650 MiB used instead of 554 MiB.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's system, c17-c22: extension toggles and VM resource commands are handler-initiated measurements. The second Windows laptop in c21 is also the reporter's own compatible setup and is folded into the same simulated user; it reproduces the same pipe errors and resource growth.

solution.intent: Disable the Windows firewall in case it is blocking communication between Podman Desktop and the running Podman machine.
solution.concrete_example: Temporarily disable the Windows firewall and check whether Podman Desktop can communicate with the machine without repeated errors.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's system, c20-c23: a firewall was proposed as a possible communication blocker; the reporter disabled it and explicitly reported no difference.

solution.intent: Treat the regression as a Podman Desktop release problem and revert Podman Desktop to the earlier 1.13.x line.
solution.concrete_example: Reinstall Podman Desktop 1.13.3 and monitor whether the repeated errors and idle CPU and memory growth stop.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's system, c21 and c24: the reporter initially suspected recent Podman Desktop versions, but reverting Podman Desktop to 1.13.3 made no difference. This failed version installation is retained as system state S2.

question_patterns: Does changing the Podman engine version affect the repeated errors and resource growth?
Can you compare the current Podman engine with the previous engine version and report what happens?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reverted Podman itself from 5.3.1 to 5.2.5. I no longer get the error in the logs, and there is no CPU or memory consumption growth.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I reverted Podman itself, but the same pipe errors and resource growth continued.
After reverting Podman, the errors stopped and resource use remained normal on only one of my two laptops.

solution.intent: Test the Podman engine as the changed component by reverting it while leaving the Podman Desktop installation in place.
solution.concrete_example: Revert Podman itself from 5.3.1 to the prior 5.2.5 installation, restart Podman Desktop, and monitor both the logs and resource usage.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's system, c24: after the Podman Desktop downgrade failed, the reporter persistently changed the Podman engine from 5.3.1 to 5.2.5 and reported the raw outcome. This introduces the successful comparison before the terminal diagnosis and creates system state S3.

solution.intent: Keep the verified Podman engine downgrade as the resolution and attribute the resource growth to the engine-version-dependent named-pipe reconnection loop rather than to activity inside the WSL machine.
solution.concrete_example: Keep Podman 5.2.5 with Podman Desktop and confirm over the previous 30–60 minute reproduction interval that the `podman-machine-default` pipe errors, CPU load, and memory growth remain absent.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the repeated ENOENT/reconnect logs and the controlled engine-version outcome. The maintainer inferred that an unstable connection causes Podman Desktop to reconnect repeatedly and create new Dockerode instances that may not be garbage-collected, accounting for both CPU load and memory growth.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's resolution from c24, grounded in the maintainer's analysis in c13: the successful engine downgrade is retained after verification. The later c25-c36 reports describe other participants' setups, including a separate Azure Kubernetes/Python process problem, and are deliberately not spliced into this reporter's causal chain.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted trigger as the Podman engine update interacting with the Podman extension, not workload inside the idle WSL machine.
Diagnosis must be grounded in the repeated `podman-machine-default` pipe ENOENT and five-second reconnect logs, the extension-isolation test, and the low resource usage inside the Podman machine.
Must recommend retaining the reporter-verified Podman engine downgrade and must not claim that downgrading Podman Desktop to 1.13.3 fixes the issue.
Must not present disabling the Windows firewall as the fix because it was tried without changing the errors or resource growth.
Must ask the user to verify that the pipe errors, CPU load, and memory growth remain absent over the previous reproduction interval before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable Windows user who can manage Scoop package versions, inspect WSL and Podman machine resources, collect Process Monitor traces, run PowerShell commands, inspect logs, and isolate extensions.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, evidence-driven, and cooperative; supplies raw logs and command output, tests proposed causes, distinguishes observations from personal hypotheses, and follows up when reproduction takes a long time.
